title: The man who ran after peace

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? is there someone you’ve stopped talking to, or two people you love who have?
options: then this one is for you. listen.
then you know how heavy it gets. listen.
good. keep this one for when it happens.

steps.line: The rabbis tell about Aaron, the brother of Moses. Whenever two people had quarreled and stopped speaking, Aaron went quietly to work.
steps.label: a teaching of the rabbis

steps.line: He sat with the first one and said, “Your friend is heartbroken. He keeps saying, ‘How can I face him? I’m the one who wronged him.’”
steps.label: a teaching of the rabbis

steps.q: Aaron leaves the first friend’s tent. What do you think he does next?
o: Tells the second friend the same story
Brings the first friend to apologize
Waits for the two to cross paths
steps.why: Avot de-Rabbi Natan says he sat with the second man until the anger left his heart, and told him the very same thing. Now each believed the other was sorry.

steps.line: Then he went to the other one, sat with him, and said the very same thing.
steps.label: a teaching of the rabbis

steps.line: When the two met, they embraced and kissed each other, friends again.
steps.label: a teaching of the rabbis

steps.q: Neither friend had actually said, “I’m the one who wronged him.” What does the Talmud teach about words like Aaron’s?
o: Any untruth is wrong, even for peace
You may change words for the sake of peace
Only a judge may bend the truth
steps.why: “One may change words for the sake of peace” (Yevamot 65b). It even shows God softening Sarah’s words when repeating them to Abraham. Readers still debate how far that goes.

steps.line: Centuries later, the great teacher Hillel said: “Be like the students of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace.”

steps.q: When Aaron died, the Torah says “all the house of Israel” wept for him. Why, say the rabbis, “all”?
o: The whole nation had seen his miracles
He had served as their high priest
He’d made peace in so many homes
steps.why: For Moses it says only “the children of Israel.” Rashi explains: Aaron made peace between friends and between husbands and wives, so everyone, men and women alike, wept for him.

steps.line: The Hebrew word for peace is shalom. It comes from a root that means whole, complete, nothing missing. Jews say it for hello, for goodbye, and for peace.

steps.q: The Talmud says Shalom is one of God’s names. Because of that, there’s one place you shouldn’t greet someone with “shalom.” Where?
steps.why: Gideon named his altar “God is Shalom” (Judges 6:24), so the rabbis taught not to greet with it in a bathhouse (Shabbat 10b). A hello that’s also a name of God.

steps.line: Today, many Jews greet each other with “shalom,” and on the day of rest, “Shabbat shalom.” Underneath the hello is an old wish: may you be whole.
steps.label: today

say: here’s what i love. aaron didn’t wait for the two of them to sort it out. he went from tent to tent.
an old psalm says, “seek peace, and pursue it.” the rabbis noticed that verb. other good deeds you do when the chance comes to you. peace, they taught, you go after.

steps.q: In the Torah, Jacob sends his son Joseph to “see the shalom of your brothers.” From what you learned, what is he asking?
o: Whether they were whole and well
steps.why: How whole are they? It’s painful to read: the brothers Joseph went to check on sold him the day he found them. Their shalom was already broken.

today.say: think of two people near you who aren’t speaking, or someone you’ve drifted from. today, take one small step toward peace: a short message, or passing on something kind and true that one of them said about the other.
options: then you’re one of aaron’s students now.
then start smaller. say shalom, and mean: may you be whole.

tomorrow.line: an old man on his last night asks his sons one thing. their answer is six words jews still say every day.

sources: Avot de-Rabbi Natan, version A, chapter 12 (when two men quarreled, Aaron sat with each in turn and said his fellow was tearing his heart, ashamed of having wronged him; when they met they embraced and kissed)
Mishnah Avot 1:12 (Hillel: be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace)
Psalms 34:15 (“Seek peace, and pursue it,” JPS 1917)
Leviticus Rabbah 9:9 (other commandments when the chance comes; peace you pursue)
Genesis 37:14 (go now, see whether it is well with thy brethren, literally ‘see the shalom of your brothers’)
Hebrew root sh-l-m (shalom, shalem: whole, complete)
check: Aaron’s words are paraphrased from Avot de-Rabbi Natan A 12; the lesson does not raise that what he told each friend was not strictly true (compare Yevamot 65b on changing words for the sake of peace)
